entities.name: Oliver Hazard Perry
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Oliver Hazard Perry (1785–1819) was a pivotal United States Navy commodore whose decisive victory at the Battle of Lake Erie in 1813 fundamentally altered the strategic landscape of the War of 1812, securing American control over the Great Lakes and significantly weakening British and Native American alliances in the Northwest Territory. Born into a distinguished naval family in South Kingstown, Rhode Island, Perry's early career was shaped by the burgeoning American maritime power and the geopolitical tensions of the early 19th century, marking him as a key figure in the nation's struggle for sovereignty and expansion.

Perry's most celebrated achievement occurred on September 10, 1813, when, commanding a hastily constructed fleet of nine ships against a more experienced British squadron under Robert Heriot Barclay, he engaged in a brutal three-hour battle near Put-in-Bay, Ohio. After his flagship, USS Lawrence, was disabled, Perry famously transferred his command to the USS Niagara and pressed the attack, ultimately forcing the surrender of the entire British fleet. His dispatch, 'We have met the enemy and they are ours,' became an iconic declaration of American naval prowess and a rallying cry for the war effort, directly leading to William Henry Harrison's victory at the Battle of the Thames.

The strategic triumph on Lake Erie had profound and immediate consequences, forcing the British to retreat from Detroit and enabling American forces to reclaim lost territory in the Northwest. It severely disrupted British supply lines and isolated their Native American allies, most notably Tecumseh's confederacy, which suffered a critical blow with Tecumseh's death shortly thereafter. Perry's victory solidified American claims to the Great Lakes frontier, influencing subsequent border negotiations and contributing to the eventual expansion of the United States westward.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Oliver Hazard Perry's decisive victory at the Battle of Lake Erie shifted the strategic balance of the War of 1812, directly leading to the collapse of Native American resistance in the Northwest and securing American control over a vital frontier. His actions had a lasting impact on U.S. territorial integrity and national identity.
